content.content:
## Beyond the Words on the Page

Reading is not a passive activity. When you read critically, you are not simply absorbing information like a sponge soaking up water. You are wrestling with ideas, questioning assumptions, evaluating evidence, and forming your own judgments. You are having a conversation with the author -- sometimes agreeing, sometimes pushing back, always thinking.

Most of the reading you do in daily life is surface reading. You scan headlines, skim social media posts, and absorb information without much reflection. This is fine for casual consumption, but it is dangerously inadequate when the stakes are higher. When a politician makes a claim about immigration, when a company advertises a product, when a news article reports on a scientific study, when a friend shares a "fact" they found online -- these moments demand critical reading.

Critical reading is a set of specific, learnable skills. It is not about being negative or suspicious of everything. It is about being thoughtful, asking the right questions, and making informed judgments. A critical reader can enjoy a beautifully written article and still notice its logical gaps. They can appreciate a persuasive speech and still identify its manipulative techniques. They can read two contradictory sources and figure out which one is more reliable.

In a world drowning in information, critical reading is not a luxury. It is survival.

## Critical Analysis: Asking the Right Questions

Critical analysis begins with a set of questions that you bring to every text. These questions peel back the surface of a text to reveal its underlying structure, assumptions, and purpose.

**Who wrote this, and why?** Every text has an author with a purpose. A climate report by an oil company has a different purpose than one by an environmental organization. A personal blog post about immigration has a different purpose than an academic study. Neither is automatically wrong, but understanding the purpose helps you anticipate potential biases and evaluate the text more effectively.

**What claims does the text make?** Identify the main argument and the supporting claims. Are these claims of fact (verifiable), claims of value (expressing a judgment), or claims of policy (proposing action)? Each type requires different evidence. A claim of fact needs data and verification. A claim of value needs ethical reasoning. A claim of policy needs both evidence and a compelling vision of the outcome.

**What evidence supports these claims?** Look for specific data, named sources, logical reasoning, and concrete examples. Be wary of vague appeals ("everyone knows," "studies show"), unsupported generalizations ("all politicians are corrupt"), and emotional manipulation in place of evidence. Strong texts show their work -- they name their sources, cite specific data, and connect evidence to claims through clear reasoning.

**What is missing?** This is perhaps the most powerful question. Every text makes choices about what to include and what to omit. A news article about a protest might focus on the violence while ignoring the peaceful majority. A company's annual report might highlight growth while downplaying debt. An opinion piece might present one side of a debate as though the other side does not exist. What the text leaves out is often as revealing as what it includes.

**What assumptions does the text make?** Every argument rests on assumptions -- beliefs or premises that the author takes for granted. An article arguing that schools should assign more homework assumes that homework improves learning. An advertisement featuring a happy family assumes that their product is associated with happiness. Identifying assumptions allows you to evaluate whether the argument holds up if those assumptions are challenged.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Why is asking "What is missing?" one of the most powerful critical reading questions?

options.text: Because all texts have typos and errors
Because most authors forget to include important information
Because what a text omits can be as revealing as what it includes
Because it helps you find additional sources

questions.solution: Every text makes deliberate choices about what to include and what to leave out. These omissions often reveal the author's bias, purpose, or perspective. A news article that focuses on protest violence while ignoring peaceful protesters, for example, creates a specific narrative through selective inclusion.

questions.task: An article argues that "schools should ban mobile phones because they distract students." What underlying assumption does this argument rely on?

options.text: That all students own mobile phones
That schools have the legal right to ban phones
That students agree phones should be banned
That the distraction caused by phones outweighs any educational benefit they provide

questions.solution: The argument assumes that the negative effects of phones (distraction) are more significant than any potential benefits (educational apps, communication, research). If this assumption is challenged -- by showing, for example, that phones enhance learning when used properly -- the argument weakens significantly.

questions.task: What is the difference between a claim of fact and a claim of value?

options.text: Claims of fact are verifiable; claims of value express judgments
Claims of fact are true; claims of value are false
Claims of fact are about science; claims of value are about art
Claims of fact are objective; claims of value are subjective and therefore unreliable

questions.solution: Claims of fact can be verified through data and evidence (e.g., "Norway's population is 5.4 million"). Claims of value express judgments or evaluations (e.g., "Norway is the best country to live in"). Both can be argued for, but they require different types of support.

## Persuasive Techniques: How Writers Influence You

Persuasion is the art of changing someone's mind or motivating them to act. It is used by advertisers, politicians, journalists, activists, and anyone who wants to influence how you think or what you do. Understanding persuasive techniques does not make you immune to them -- but it makes you aware, which is the first step to thinking independently.

**Ethos** is persuasion through credibility. When a doctor recommends a treatment, their expertise lends weight to the recommendation. When a celebrity endorses a product, their fame (though not necessarily their expertise) creates trust. When a writer cites peer-reviewed studies, they establish themselves as a serious, well-informed source. Ethos appeals to the question: "Can I trust this person?"

**Pathos** is persuasion through emotion. A charity advertisement showing a hungry child creates sympathy and guilt that motivate donations. A political speech recounting a personal tragedy creates empathy and urgency. Music in a film builds suspense, joy, or sorrow. Pathos is powerful because emotions drive decisions more than logic does -- studies show that people decide first with their feelings and then look for rational justifications.

**Logos** is persuasion through logic and evidence. Statistics, expert opinions, logical reasoning, and empirical data all appeal to logos. "This policy reduced crime by 30% in cities that adopted it" is a logos-based argument. Logos works best when the audience values rationality and has time to evaluate the evidence. In quick-decision contexts (like advertising), pathos tends to dominate.

**Repetition** embeds ideas through frequency. If you hear a slogan enough times, it starts to feel true whether or not it is. Advertisers know this. Politicians know this. Social media algorithms know this. The mere familiarity of a claim can make it feel more credible -- psychologists call this the "illusory truth effect."

**Bandwagon appeal** creates pressure to join the majority. "Nine out of ten dentists recommend..." "Join the millions who have already switched..." "Everyone is talking about..." These phrases imply that if so many people agree, you should too. The logic is flawed, but the social pressure is real.

**Scarcity and urgency** create pressure to act immediately. "Limited time offer!" "Only 3 left in stock!" "This deal expires tonight!" These techniques exploit the fear of missing out and short-circuit careful evaluation. If you feel rushed to make a decision, that is usually a sign to slow down and think critically.

questions.task: A charity shows a video of suffering animals with sad music playing. Which persuasive technique is primarily being used?

options.text: Logos -- appealing to logic and data
Pathos -- appealing to emotions
Ethos -- establishing credibility
Bandwagon -- suggesting everyone is donating

questions.solution: The combination of visual suffering and sad music is a pathos-based appeal, designed to create emotional responses of sympathy, guilt, and urgency that motivate donations. Pathos is particularly effective because emotions drive decisions more powerfully than logic alone.

options.text: The tendency to believe experts are always right
The tendency to believe things that are written rather than spoken
The tendency for repeated claims to feel more credible simply due to familiarity
The tendency to accept visual evidence over written evidence

questions.solution: The illusory truth effect is a psychological phenomenon where repeated exposure to a claim makes it feel more true, regardless of its actual accuracy. This is why propaganda and advertising rely heavily on repetition -- familiarity breeds a sense of credibility.

## Evaluation and Synthesis: Building Your Own Understanding

The ultimate goal of critical reading is not just to evaluate individual texts but to synthesize information from multiple sources into a coherent, well-informed understanding. Synthesis is the highest level of critical thinking -- it means taking different pieces of information, identifying patterns and contradictions, and constructing your own informed perspective.

**Evaluation** is the process of judging a text's quality, reliability, and relevance. After analyzing a text (identifying its claims, evidence, purpose, and techniques), you evaluate it: Is the evidence strong enough to support the claims? Is the reasoning logical? Is the source credible? Are important perspectives missing? Evaluation is not about whether you agree with the text but about whether the text makes its case effectively.

**Comparison** is the bridge between evaluation and synthesis. When you read multiple texts on the same topic, you compare their claims, evidence, perspectives, and conclusions. Where do they agree? Where do they disagree? What evidence does one include that the other omits? Comparison reveals the complexity of issues that any single source might simplify.

**Synthesis** takes comparison further. It means integrating information from multiple sources to create a new, more complete understanding. Imagine you read five articles about social media's impact on teenagers. One focuses on mental health risks, another on social connection benefits, a third on academic effects, a fourth on political engagement, and a fifth on privacy concerns. Synthesis means weaving these five perspectives into a nuanced understanding that no single article provided.

When writing a synthesis, avoid simply summarizing each source in turn ("Source A says... Source B says... Source C says..."). Instead, organize by themes or arguments. "Research on social media's impact on teenagers reveals a complex picture. While evidence suggests significant mental health risks, including increased anxiety and depression (Smith, 2023), other studies highlight genuine social benefits, such as maintaining friendships across distances and finding supportive communities (Johnson, 2022). The challenge lies in maximizing these benefits while mitigating the harms."

This approach shows that you have processed the sources, identified patterns, and formed your own perspective. It demonstrates thinking, not just reading -- and that is what critical reading is all about.

exercise.task: Test yourself on evaluation and synthesis:

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What is the difference between comparison and synthesis?

options.text: Comparison looks at similarities; synthesis looks at differences
Comparison is for academic writing; synthesis is for creative writing
They are the same thing described in different words
Comparison examines multiple sources side by side; synthesis integrates them into a new, more complete understanding

questions.solution: Comparison is examining multiple sources side by side to identify agreements, disagreements, and gaps. Synthesis goes further by integrating those different perspectives into a new, more nuanced understanding. Synthesis creates something new from the raw material of comparison.

questions.task: When writing a synthesis, why should you organize by themes rather than summarizing each source in turn?

options.text: Because thematic organization shows you have processed the sources and formed your own perspective
Because it makes the text shorter
Because organizing by source is considered plagiarism
Because sources might disagree with each other and this avoids the conflict

questions.solution: Organizing by themes demonstrates that you have actually synthesized the information -- processed, compared, and integrated it into your own understanding. Source-by-source summaries suggest you have simply read the sources without engaging critically. Thematic organization shows thinking, not just reading.

content.content:
## Summary

**Critical reading** is an active, questioning process of engaging with texts. It begins with **critical analysis** -- asking who wrote this and why, what claims are made, what evidence supports them, what is missing, and what assumptions underlie the argument.

**Persuasive techniques** include ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion), logos (logic), repetition (which creates the illusory truth effect), bandwagon appeal, and scarcity/urgency tactics. Recognizing these techniques helps you evaluate how writers influence your thinking.

The highest level of critical reading is **synthesis** -- integrating information from multiple sources into a new, more complete understanding. Effective synthesis organizes by themes rather than by source, demonstrating that you have processed, compared, and integrated the information into your own informed perspective. In a world overflowing with competing claims and information, critical reading is not a luxury -- it is essential for informed citizenship.
